source.name: OER Commons — Constitutional Law & Human Rights

course.title: Constitutional Law & Human Rights
course.description: A global, comparative introduction to how constitutions organize power and protect people — from constitutionalism and the separation of powers to the rule of law, fundamental rights, equality, and international human rights. Built from openly-licensed OER Commons material (CC BY). This course is legal literacy, not legal advice: it explains general principles and does not address any specific situation or jurisdiction.

questions.prompt: A constitution is best described as…
options: the framework that establishes and limits a state's power
questions.explanation: Constitutions set up the organs of government and set limits on their power — covered in 'What a constitution is'.

questions.prompt: 'Separation of powers' primarily divides government into…
questions.explanation: The classic three-branch division — see 'Separation of powers'.

questions.prompt: The 'rule of law' means, above all, that…
options: the ruler makes all law personally
everyone, including the government, is bound by law
questions.explanation: No one is above the law, including officials — see 'Rule of law and judicial review'.

questions.prompt: Judicial review is the power of courts to…
options: review whether laws or acts comply with the constitution
questions.explanation: Courts test official acts against the constitution — see 'Rule of law and judicial review'.

questions.prompt: Which is a classic civil liberty?
options: the right to a government job
questions.explanation: Freedom of expression is a core liberty — see 'Fundamental rights'.

questions.prompt: The principle of equality before the law means…
options: the law applies to like cases alike, without arbitrary discrimination
questions.explanation: Equal treatment and non-discrimination — see 'Fundamental rights'.

questions.prompt: The 1948 document that set out a shared list of human rights globally is the…
questions.explanation: The UDHR — see 'International human rights'.

questions.prompt: Most rights are…
options: often limited, but only by law and for legitimate, proportionate reasons
questions.explanation: Limitation must be lawful, necessary, and proportionate — a recurring theme in this course.

lessons.title: What a constitution is (and constitutionalism)
lessons.grammar_note: Two senses of 'constitution': the document, and the deeper practice of limited government (constitutionalism).

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Define a constitution, distinguish it from ordinary law, and explain constitutionalism. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, what two things does a constitution do to power — and which of them is the harder one to guarantee?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A *constitution* is the highest-ranking framework of a state: it creates the main institutions, distributes power among them, and sets limits on how that power may be used. Constitutions come in different forms — some codified in a single document (as in most countries), some uncodified and spread across statutes, cases, and conventions (as in the United Kingdom). *Constitutionalism* is the deeper commitment behind the text: the idea that government power should be limited, accountable, and exercised according to known rules rather than personal will. A country can have a written constitution without genuine constitutionalism if those limits are ignored in practice.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Reasoning through a rights scenario: imagine an official orders a newspaper closed overnight because it criticized her. To evaluate this you don't start with your opinion — you ask constitutional questions. Does the constitution grant this official that power? Does it protect press freedom? Is there a lawful procedure and a right to challenge the order in court? If power was used outside its granted limits and without process, that is a failure of constitutionalism, whatever the document says.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Classify each as (a) codified feature, (b) constitutionalism value, or (c) neither: (1) a single written charter listing the branches of government; (2) the expectation that a president obeys a court ruling against her; (3) a company's staff handbook; (4) an unwritten convention that the losing side concedes an election; (5) a tax form. Answers: 1-a, 2-b, 3-c, 4-b, 5-c.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming any country with a written constitution automatically has limited government — the practice matters as much as the text. Mistake: thinking 'unwritten' means 'no constitution' — it means the rules live in many sources. Exit: (a) In one word, what does constitutionalism place on power? (b) Name one form a constitution can take other than a single codified document. Answers: limits; an uncodified set of statutes, cases, and conventions.

lessons.title: Separation of powers & checks and balances
lessons.grammar_note: Separation = dividing functions; checks and balances = each branch can restrain the others.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Name the three branches, explain why power is separated, and give an example of a check. Warm-up: which branch makes law, which applies it, and which interprets disputes about it?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: To stop power concentrating in one set of hands, most constitutions divide government into a *legislature* (makes law), an *executive* (carries it out), and a *judiciary* (resolves disputes and interprets law). *Checks and balances* let each branch restrain the others: a court can strike down an unconstitutional act, a legislature can amend law or hold the executive to account, and an executive may have a limited veto. Systems differ — *presidential* systems (e.g. the United States, Brazil) keep the executive and legislature separately elected, while *parliamentary* systems (e.g. Germany, India, Japan) fuse them, with a government drawn from and answerable to parliament. The shared goal is accountability, not gridlock for its own sake.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Reasoning through a rights scenario: a government wants to detain protesters without charge for 90 days and passes a statute to allow it. Trace the checks. The legislature debated and could have refused or amended the bill. If it passed, individuals may ask the judiciary whether indefinite detention without charge violates constitutional liberty guarantees; a court can invalidate or narrow the statute. Elections let voters remove the executive later. No single branch has the last word alone — that dispersal is the point.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Match each act to a branch — legislature, executive, or judiciary: (1) signing a treaty into effect; (2) ruling a law unconstitutional; (3) passing a budget; (4) enforcing a court order through the police; (5) amending a statute. Answers: 1-executive, 2-judiciary, 3-legislature, 4-executive, 5-legislature.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking separation means the branches never interact — checks and balances require interaction. Mistake: assuming all democracies use the presidential model — parliamentary systems fuse executive and legislature by design. Exit: (a) Which branch typically interprets whether an act is constitutional? (b) Name one difference between presidential and parliamentary systems. Answers: the judiciary; in parliamentary systems the executive is drawn from and answerable to the legislature, not separately elected.

lessons.title: Rule of law & judicial review
lessons.grammar_note: Rule of law is the standard; judicial review is one tool that enforces it.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: State the core elements of the rule of law and explain what judicial review checks. Warm-up: if the government itself breaks a law, what does the rule of law say should happen?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The *rule of law* holds that everyone — private people and public officials alike — is subject to law that is public, prospective, clear, and applied by independent courts. Its usual elements include legality (officials act only on legal authority), equality before the law, legal certainty, access to justice, and an independent judiciary. *Judicial review* is one mechanism that enforces these ideas: courts examine whether a law or government act conforms to the constitution or to legal limits, and may set it aside if it does not. Approaches vary — some countries use a specialized *constitutional court* (Germany, South Africa), others let ordinary courts decide constitutional questions (the United States, Kenya, India) — but the function is similar: measuring power against a higher legal standard.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Reasoning through a rights scenario: a ministry cancels the passports of citizens who criticized it abroad, citing 'national interest' but pointing to no statute. Test it against the rule of law. Legality: is there a legal basis? None is named. Certainty: was the rule knowable in advance? No. Equality: is it applied evenhandedly, or aimed at critics? Independent review: can the citizens challenge it in court? If the act has no legal basis, targets a group, and escapes review, it fails the rule of law — and judicial review is the route to test it.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Which rule-of-law element is most at risk in each case? (1) A law punishes conduct that was legal when it was done. (2) A judge takes orders from the president on how to rule. (3) A statute is written so vaguely no one can tell what it forbids. (4) Court fees are so high ordinary people cannot sue. Answers: 1-legality/non-retroactivity, 2-judicial independence, 3-legal certainty/clarity, 4-access to justice.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: confusing 'rule of law' with 'rule by law' — a government can pass many laws and still be lawless if those laws are secret, retroactive, or unreviewable. Mistake: assuming only one country's model of judicial review exists. Exit: (a) Name two elements of the rule of law. (b) What does judicial review compare an official act against? Answers: e.g. legality and an independent judiciary; the constitution or higher legal limits.

questions.prompt: Constitutionalism is best summarized as…
options: the practice of limited, accountable government under known rules
questions.explanation: It is the commitment to limits on power, not merely a text.

questions.prompt: In a parliamentary system, the executive is…
options: drawn from and answerable to the legislature
questions.explanation: Parliamentary systems fuse executive and legislature.

questions.prompt: Striking down an unconstitutional statute is a check exercised by the…
questions.explanation: Judicial review is a judicial check.

questions.prompt: Punishing an act that was lawful when committed mainly violates…
questions.explanation: Retroactive punishment breaks legal certainty.

questions.prompt: 'Rule by law' differs from 'rule of law' because rule by law can still be…
options: arbitrary if laws are secret, retroactive, or unreviewable
questions.explanation: Many laws do not guarantee lawfulness.

questions.prompt: A specialized constitutional court is used by countries such as…
questions.explanation: Some states centralize constitutional review in one court.

lessons.title: Fundamental rights, civil liberties & equality
lessons.grammar_note: Rights are usually limitable: a limit must be prescribed by law, pursue a legitimate aim, and be proportionate.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Distinguish kinds of rights, apply a limitation test, and explain equality and non-discrimination. Warm-up: is freedom of expression an absolute right, or one that can be limited — and if it can be limited, what should a fair limit require?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: *Fundamental rights* protect people against abuses of power and secure conditions for a dignified life. They are often grouped as *civil and political rights* (expression, assembly, religion, fair trial, privacy, the vote) and *economic, social and cultural rights* (education, health, work). Most rights are not absolute: they can be limited, but a legitimate limit is usually *prescribed by law*, serves a *legitimate aim* (such as public safety or the rights of others), and is *proportionate* — no more restrictive than necessary. A narrow core, such as the prohibition of torture, is treated as *absolute* and cannot be balanced away. *Equality before the law* and *non-discrimination* run through all of this: like cases should be treated alike, and distinctions based on grounds such as race, sex, religion, or disability require strong justification.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Reasoning through a rights scenario: a city bans all demonstrations in the main square for six months after one protest turned disorderly. Apply the limitation test. Prescribed by law? Suppose a public-order statute allows restrictions — yes. Legitimate aim? Public safety — yes. Proportionate? A blanket six-month ban on all protest by everyone is likely more than necessary; a narrower rule (limited times, routes, or notice requirements) would achieve safety with less cost to assembly. So the aim is legitimate but the measure probably fails proportionality — the reasoning, not the slogan, decides it.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: For each limit, name the limitation step most in doubt — lawful basis, legitimate aim, or proportionality: (1) banning a peaceful vigil purely because officials dislike the message; (2) a night-time noise rule that quiets loudspeakers after 11pm but allows daytime rallies; (3) detaining a journalist with no statute authorizing it; (4) requiring 30 days' notice for any gathering of two or more people. Answers: 1-legitimate aim (dislike of a message is not legitimate), 2-passes (proportionate and legitimate), 3-lawful basis, 4-proportionality.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking all rights are absolute — most can be limited under a proper test; only a small core (e.g. the ban on torture) cannot. Mistake: treating equality as identical treatment in every case — treating genuinely different situations differently, or making reasonable accommodations, can be what equality requires. Exit: (a) Name the three parts of a standard limitation test. (b) Give one right usually treated as absolute. Answers: prescribed by law, legitimate aim, proportionate; the prohibition of torture.

lessons.title: International human rights: the UDHR and key instruments
lessons.grammar_note: A declaration sets standards; a treaty (covenant/convention) creates binding obligations for states that ratify it.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain what the UDHR is, distinguish declarations from treaties, and name major human rights instruments. Warm-up: the UDHR was adopted in 1948 — does that date make its rights automatically enforceable in every national court?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: After the Second World War, states built a shared framework of *international human rights*. The *Universal Declaration of Human Rights* (UDHR, 1948) is a milestone *declaration*: it proclaims a common standard of rights but is not itself a binding treaty. Its principles were later put into binding *treaties* — most importantly the *International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights* (ICCPR) and the *International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights* (ICESCR), both 1966. Further conventions target specific concerns: against racial discrimination (CERD), against discrimination against women (CEDAW), against torture (CAT), and on the rights of the child (CRC). Regional systems add courts and charters — the European, Inter-American, and African systems each protect rights across their regions. A state generally becomes bound when it *ratifies* a treaty; enforcement then runs through domestic courts and international monitoring bodies.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Reasoning through a rights scenario: an activist says 'the UDHR guarantees my right to health, so my national court must order the treatment.' Reason it through. The UDHR is a declaration, so it sets a standard but does not by itself bind courts. The binding source would be a treaty the state ratified (e.g. the ICESCR) and, crucially, how that treaty has been made part of national law. So the right exists at the level of international standards, but whether a domestic court can enforce it depends on ratification and incorporation — the analysis matters more than the headline.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Label each as a declaration, a global treaty, or a regional system: (1) the UDHR; (2) the ICCPR; (3) the Inter-American human rights system; (4) CEDAW; (5) the African human rights system. Answers: 1-declaration, 2-global treaty, 3-regional system, 4-global treaty, 5-regional system.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating the UDHR as a binding treaty — it is a foundational declaration whose norms were later codified in treaties. Mistake: assuming ratifying a treaty automatically makes it enforceable in every national court — much depends on how each state incorporates it. Exit: (a) What is the difference between a declaration and a treaty? (b) Name the two 1966 covenants. Answers: a declaration sets standards while a treaty binds states that ratify it; the ICCPR and the ICESCR.

items.translation: the principle that government power should be limited, accountable, and exercised under known rules
items.example: A written charter without constitutionalism is text that officials feel free to ignore.

items.translation: dividing government functions among legislative, executive, and judicial branches so no one branch dominates
items.example: Separation of powers is reinforced by checks and balances between the branches.

items.translation: the standard that everyone, including the government, is bound by public, clear, and independently applied law
items.example: The rule of law fails when officials act with no legal basis.

items.translation: a court's power to test whether a law or official act complies with the constitution or higher legal limits
items.example: Through judicial review a court may set aside an unconstitutional statute.

items.translation: the requirement that a limit on a right be no more restrictive than necessary to achieve a legitimate aim
items.example: A blanket six-month protest ban likely fails proportionality.

items.translation: the 1948 declaration proclaiming a common standard of human rights, later codified in binding treaties
items.example: The UDHR inspired the ICCPR and the ICESCR of 1966.

questions.prompt: A standard limitation on a right must be prescribed by law, pursue a legitimate aim, and be…
questions.explanation: Proportionality is the third step.

questions.prompt: Which right is usually treated as absolute?
questions.explanation: The ban on torture cannot be balanced away.

questions.prompt: The UDHR (1948) is a…
questions.explanation: It is a declaration, later codified in treaties.

questions.prompt: The two 1966 covenants are the ICCPR and the…
questions.explanation: Civil-political and economic-social-cultural covenants.

questions.prompt: Equality before the law requires that…
options: like cases be treated alike, with distinctions needing strong justification
questions.explanation: Non-arbitrary treatment, not identical outcomes.

questions.prompt: A state generally becomes bound by a human rights treaty when it…
questions.explanation: Ratification creates the binding obligation.

lessons.title: Applied project: analyze a rights question

sections.heading: The task
sections.text: Choose a general, hypothetical rights question — for example, 'may a government restrict a public protest during a health emergency?' — and analyze it using the constitutional principles from this course. You are not giving legal advice or resolving a real dispute; you are practicing structured legal reasoning about a general scenario.

sections.heading: Milestones
sections.text: 1) State the scenario and the right(s) involved in one or two sentences. 2) Identify whose power is being used and whether a constitution or law appears to grant it (legality and separation of powers). 3) Apply the limitation test: is the measure prescribed by law, does it serve a legitimate aim, and is it proportionate? 4) Note any equality or non-discrimination concern. 5) Say which body could review the measure and against what standard (the constitution or a ratified human rights treaty).

sections.heading: Self-check rubric
sections.text: ✔ You named the specific right(s) rather than speaking only of 'freedom' in general. ✔ You separated the question of power (who may act, and under what authority) from the question of limits. ✔ You ran the full limitation test and reasoned about proportionality, not just the aim. ✔ You identified a review body and the standard it would apply. ✔ You framed your answer as general legal literacy — comparative and non-partisan — and avoided claiming it as advice for any actual case. If all five hold, you have reasoned like a constitutional lawyer without pretending to be anyone's.
